UNITED NATIONS 
DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK 
2002-2006 
THE GAMBIA 
31 DECEMBER 2000 PREFACE 
The UN system in The Gambia, in line with 
the global effort of the United Nations, is 
developing a common planning framework, 
which will ensure greater impact of its 
development interventions in support of the 
objectives of Sustainable Human 
Development. The General Assembly 
resolution 53/192, which came after 
discussions during the 1998 triennial policy 
review, emphasised the need for the full 
participation and direct involvement of 
governments and all parts of the UN system in 
the United Nations Development Assistance 
Framework (UNDAF) process. In order to 
develop a common development assistance 
framework, the first step is the preparation of 
the Common Country Assessment (CCA). 
 
The CCA for The Gambia, which was 
produced in mid-1999, provides a common 
database on The Gambia’s demographic, 
social, economic, health, educational and other 
indicators necessary for the programming 
activities of the UN agencies. A broad-based 
task force comprising all UN agencies, 
Departments of State, National Environment 
Agency, National Population Commission 
Secretariat, Central Statistics Department, 
Women’s Bureau, NGO Affairs Agency, and 
TANGO was set up to co-ordinate the 
preparation of the CCA. This was done under 
the Resident Co-ordinator system while the 
Central Statistics Department (CSD) was given 
the overall responsibility of producing the 
CCA report. 
The draft CCA was the subject of a workshop 
held on 5 April 1998 aimed at soliciting inputs 
from major stakeholders. The views and 
comments emanating from this workshop were 
incorporated in the final CCA. Updating the 
CCA is the responsibility of the CSD in 
collaboration with the UN system. 
Under the UNDAF framework, the UN 
agencies in the Gambia and non-resident 
agencies based in Dakar, Senegal organised a 
retreat at Sene-Gambia Beach Hotel on 26th
and 27th October 2000, to consider and reflect 
on development priorities and collaboration 
issues between the agencies. 
The workshop successfully identified 
development priority areas for programming 
and also potential strategies to be considered in 
the development of the UNDAF for The 
Gambia. The programmes will be developed 
by the individual agencies who will consider 
the collaborative areas of programming, 
resource mobilisation, monitoring and 
evaluation and follow-up procedures for the 
UNDAF. A national workshop comprising 
the UN system, the Government, NGO 
community, civil society and donors was held 
during 15th - 16th November 2000. It provided 
a platform for wider consultation regarding the 
areas of collaboration during the UNDAF. 
The UNCT would like to take this opportunity, 
to thank all the development partners for their 
collaboration during the process of the 
UNDAF preparation, the UNDAF Task Force 
set up by the GOTG, and last but not least, the 
Inter Agency Thematic Group on Economic 
Management and Governance, which coordinated the whole exercise.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
Introduction 
The preparation of the United Nations 
Development Assistance Framework 
(UNDAF) for The Gambia, and the Common 
Country Assessment (CCA), which provides 
the foundation for the UNDAF, has brought 
greater cohesion among the UN Country 
Team. More importantly it has indicated the 
need for the UNCT to speak out with one 
voice in its advocacy with government, 
especially on issues dealing with human 
development and human rights. 
The CCA, which was completed in July 1999, 
provides invaluable information on the 
challenges facing The Gambia, as well as the 
efforts being made by the country and its 
development partners to address the same, 
including successes and failures, thereof. 
The Gambia's Vision 2020 spells out that the 
priorities of the Government lies in building 
and developing its human resources to achieve 
the highest creative potential through the 
improvement of the economic, social, political 
and environmental framework of the country. 
In this respect, a two pronged approach has 
been adopted, namely: 
• To bring about macroeconomic stability in 
order to stimulate a rapid growth of 
incomes and employment; and 
• To build human capital to enable, the poor 
to take advantage of new opportunities 
through improving their access to 
education, health, and other social 
services. 
The Government has therefore designed 
policies and programmes to meet its 
development objectives. Most of these 
policies and strategies are in the process of 
being implemented with the assistance of 
development partners, including the UN 
System. The areas covered include agriculture 
and natural resources development, industrial 
and infrastructure development, the services 
sector, human resources development, social 
sectors, advancement of women, population, 
housing, environmental protection private 
sector development, and rationalisation and 
strengthening of public sector institutions. 
This UNDAF is being prepared using a rightsbased approach for programming of 
development assistance. Human rights relate 
strongly to other major cross-cutting issues 
like poverty, gender, population and good 
governance. 
Human rights pose a major challenge on the 
development landscape and the UN system 
will under the UNDAF process formulate 
strategies and advocate for policies that ensure 
the right to development and the protection, 
promotion and development of civil, cultural, 
economic, political and social rights of The 
Gambian 
Goals and Objectives of the UNDAF 
It must be indicated that the UN System has 
been co-operating with the Government of The 
Gambia (GOTG) for over a decade. UNICEF, 
UNDP, UNFPA, WFP, WHO, FAO and 
UNHCR have their local representation in the 
country, while ILO, UNESCO, and IFAD are 
covered from either Dakar , Abidjan and 
Rome, respectively. 
According to the 1998 Development 
Cooperation Report, the UN System provided 
at total of US $37.7 million (59.2%) of the 
US$63.7 million the total external assistance 
that flowed to The Gambia in 1998. 
The main goals of the UN System in The 
Gambia are: 
• To promote human development, 
• To assist in the eradication of poverty; 
and, 
• The promotion and protection of human 
rights and good governance. 
All these objectives are consistent with the 
country's development objectives as spelled 
out in the Vision 2020 as well as the recently 
drafted strategy for Poverty Alleviation 
(SPAII) otherwise known as the Poverty 
Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP). 
Experience shows that, although the UN 
System share a common purpose in The 
Gambia, their interventions were neither coordinated nor focused. To this end, the 
UNDAF has been developed as a framework 
of UN collaboration with the Government of 
The Gambia (GOTG). The main objective of 
the UNDAF is therefore to achieve greater 
impact of UN System cooperation on the  IV
development and well-being of people,
through improved focus, and results 
orientation, identifying where using its unique 
strengths as a development partner. The 
UNDAF provides an opportunity and 
framework for co-ordination between the UN 
System, other donors, the NGO community 
and the Government. 
Areas of Cooperation 
Through the CCA and UNDAF exercises, the 
UNCT initiated a process of dialogue and 
consultations with Government and other 
development partners, which was aimed at 
narrowing the focus of, and rationalising UN 
assistance in The Gambia. The process has led 
to the identification of four areas as priority for 
UN assistance. These are: 
• Governance 
• Poverty 
• Economic management; and, 
• Environment and Natural Resources 
These four areas, which are inter-linked, and 
cross cutting, are very critical to the 
development of The Gambia. The GOTG has 
formulated national programmes and policies 
in the areas of Governance, Poverty, and 
Environment and Natural Resources. In the 
social sector area policies and strategies have 
been adopted for the advancement of women, 
youth, nutrition and education. At the same 
time, the importance of sound economic 
management, for achieving growth and 
sustainable development cannot be 
overemphasised. The relevance of these four 
key areas to the development of the agenda, 
was confirmed at the national workshop on the 
UNDAF, which took place in Banjul during 
15-16 November 2000, at which the 
framework was endorsed. 
Promotion of gender equity and fight against 
HIV/AIDS were seen as crosscutting issues 
that required attention. 
The UNDAF therefore, provides a road map, 
to reach the goals of the UN system in the 
Gambia, by identifying those areas that are 
critical to the development of the Gambia, in 
which at the same time the UN system has a 
comparative advantage. 
In formulating the UNDAF special care has 
been taken to indicate that it is not only 
consistent with the newly formulated Strategy 
for Poverty Alleviation (SPA II)/ Poverty 
Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP), and the 
ongoing Vision 2020 operationalization 
exercise, but that there is optimal synergy and 
complimentarity. 
The UNCT recognises the need for stronger 
donor coordination if at all the objectives of 
the UNDAF are to be met. In this respect, 
current efforts being undertaken by GOTG to 
strengthen donor coordination, through the 
elaboration of a donor coordination policy and 
creating/strengthening appropriate donor 
coordination institutions and mechanisms, are 
commended. 
The UNCT has agreed to take appropriate 
steps to strengthen the capacity of the UN 
system to enable it to implement and monitor 
the UNDAF and to harmonise its programmes 
of assistance (UNICEF, UNDP and UNFPA) 
by January 2002, to contribute to the full 
realisation of human development and human 
rights in the Gambia. United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for The Gambia, 2002 to2006

 1.0 RATIONALE 
One of the principal elements of the UN 
Secretary General’s reform proposals calls for 
strengthening operations of the UN System at the 
Country level through the formulation and 
presentation of a United Nations Development 
Assistance Framework (UNDAF). The UN 
system in The Gambia, in line with the global 
effort of the United Nations is developing a 
common planning framework, which will ensure 
greater impact of its development interventions 
in support of the objectives of Sustainable 
Human Development. The General Assembly 
resolution 53/192 which came after discussions 
during the 1998 triennial policy review 
emphasised the need for the full participation and 
direct involvement of governments and all parts 
of the UN system in the United Nations 
Development Framework (UNDAF) process. In 
order to develop a common development 
assistance framework, the first step is the 
preparation of the Common Country Assessment 
(CCA). 
Preparation of the UNDAF is mandatory for all 
UN Country Teams (UNCT). While its 
preparation is largely the responsibility of all UN 
Funds and Programmes (UNDP, UNICEF, 
UNFPA, WFP), specialised UN agencies and the 
Brettonwoods institutions are encouraged to 
participate, at the same time, Government 
support and participation is vital. In addition, 
donor organisations, NGOs, other civil society 
groups and professionals are invited to 
participate, making the UNDAF preparation 
process highly participatory. 
It should be noted that other programming 
frameworks/instruments also exist at the country 
level. These include the Sectoral Investment 
Programmes (SIPs), Comprehensive 
Development Framework (CDF), and the 
Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP) 
largely advocated by the Brettonwoods 
Institutions. 
The most critical element for the UNDAF is that 
drawing from the development priorities 
identified by the client country and global as 
well as regional concerns agreed at various UN 
and regional conferences, and taking into 
account the mandates and comparative 
advantaged of the various UN agencies, the 
UNCT comes up with a package of assistance 
that will best address the above concerns in a 
particular country. A common Country 
Assessment (CCA), which precedes the UNDAF 
and undertaken by the UNCT, in close 
collaboration with the Government, provides the 
analytical basis for UNDAF. UNDAF as defined 
by the United Nations is “the planning 
framework for the development operations of the 
UN system at country level. It consists of 
common objectives and strategies of 
cooperation, a programme resources framework 
and proposals for follow-up, monitoring and 
evaluation.” This falls in line with the call by 
the UN Secretary General in resolution 53/192 
for the UN system to achieve “goal-oriented 
collaboration, coherence and mutual 
reinforcement.” The UNDAF is the basis for 
establishing cooperation among UN agencies; 
the government and other development partners 
through the formulation of complementary 
programmes aimed at addressing established 
national priorities and development challenges. 
However, the UNDAF should also relate to the 
CDF, PRSP, SIPs and indeed any other country 
level development frameworks, where such exist, 
to ensure synergy and complimentarity between 
UN assistance with that of other development 
partners. 
2.0 CURRENT DEVELOPMENT 
PROBLEMS AND CHALLENGES 
2.1 Problems 
With a per capita income of about US $300 - 320 
per annum, The Gambia is classified as one of 
the Least Developed Countries in the world. The 
UNDP 2000 Human Development Report ranks 
the Gambia at 161 out of 174 countries, with a 
Human Development Index (HDI) value of 0.396 
(2000). The population is currently estimated at 
1.3 million and growing at 4.2 per cent per 
annum, one of the fastest growth rates in the 
developing world. Life expectancy at birth is 
still low at 55 years overall, and 54 years and 57 
for males and females, respectively. The 
economy is predominantly agrarian. Thus, 
although the agricultural sector contributes only 
25 per cent of GDP, it is the source of livelihood 
for over 75 per cent of the population, who 
reside in the rural areas. However, the sector is 
characterised by low productivity, stemming 
largely from over reliance on poor technology, 
and low and declining soil fertility. Structural 
and cultural problems also hamper the United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for The Gambia, 2002 to2006 
2
development of the sector. These include 
women's limited access to land, the absence of a 
rural credit network and the insufficient access of 
farmers to appropriate technology and adequate 
inputs. The Manufacturing sector is small and 
rudimentary, contributing about 10 per cent of 
GDP. The Services sector, which is dominated 
by the hotels industry and a vibrant informal 
sub-sector, contributes about 65 per cent of 
GDP, and is the main foreign exchange earner. 
The Gambia has a limited resource base, and 
infrastructure is generally underdeveloped and 
suffers from lack of maintenance. Rapid 
population growth and increasing urbanisation 
have posed a threat to the environment and put 
pressure on the limited natural resources, thus 
aggravating environmental problems such as soil 
degradation, loss of forest cover, loss of biodiversity, and poor sanitation. The basic social 
indicators clearly demonstrate pervasive poverty 
in the country. For example, only 50 per cent of 
the population have access to clean drinking 
water. According to the 1998 Household Poverty 
Survey, 37 per cent of Gambian households and 
51 per cent of the population are extremely poor. 
At the same time, in the area of education, 
enrolment rates are low, albeit improving, 
particularly among girls. According to the 
Education For All 2000 Assessment Report, in 
1998/99 the overall gross enrolment ratio (GER) 
stood at 71.7 per cent as compared to 59 per cent 
in 1991/91. During the same period, the GERs 
for males and females rose from 70 to 78 per 
cent and 47.9 to 65.6 per cent, respectively. 
Literacy levels (15-24 age group) are very low, 
with the overall illiteracy level standing at 63 per 
cent and that for females at 75 per cent (1998). 
Latest health statistics indicate that although as 
much as 90 per cent of the Gambian population 
have access to health services, the majority of the 
rural population cannot access health facilities if 
we take into consideration affordability of 
transport costs and drug recovery charges. The 
incidence of malnutrition is quite high with 
children being the most affected group, while 
under-five mortality estimated at 192 per 1,000 
(1993), is one of the highest in the sub-region, 
albeit on a declining trend. In addition, rapid 
population growth, coupled with slow economic 
expansion over the years has resulted in a 
decrease in employment opportunities for a 
growing labour force, while under-employment 
and low productivity are rampant in the rural 
areas. Unemployment, particularly among the 
youth in urban areas, is a very serious concern. 
2.2 Challenges 
From the above, it is obvious that the Gambia 
faces very serious development challenges which 
will need to be addressed both in the short 
medium and the long term. These include (a) 
pervasive poverty; (b) food insecurity; (c) 
environmental degradation; (d) underdeveloped 
human resources; (e) high population growth, (f) 
the AIDS pandemic ; and (g) Poor Governance. 
The Gambia’s primary development challenge is 
to eradicate poverty and promote sustainable and 
equitable development. To this end, a number of 
policies, strategies and programmes have been 
developed to address these challenges. The 
Programme for Sustained Development (PSD) 
and Vision 2020 are the main strategy 
documents outlining the Gambia’s medium and 
long-term development objectives, which can be 
summarised as follows: 
• “to transform the Gambia into a financial 
centre, a tourist paradise, a trading, exportoriented agricultural and manufacturing 
nation, thriving on free market policies and 
a vibrant private sector, sustained by a well 
educated, trained, skilled, healthy, selfreliant and enterprising population, and 
guaranteeing a well-balanced ecosystem 
and a decent standard of living for one and 
FOOD SECURITY 
According to the World Food Summit, food security 
exists when all people, at all times, have physical and 
economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious 
food to meet their dietary needs and food preferences 
for an active and healthy life. Achieving food 
security means ensuring that sufficient food is 
available, that supplies are relatively stable and that 
those in need of food can obtain it. 
In The Gambia 51% of the population is classified as 
extremely poor (1998 National Household Poverty 
Survey). The incidence of food insecurity in this part 
of the population is high. The main reasons for 
insufficient access to food are low and nondiversified agricultural production of rural 
households and low income levels. Also unequal 
distribution of food within households affects 
especially women and children.United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for The Gambia, 2002 to2006

all, under a system of government based on 
the consent of the citizenry”.1 
 
In order to address the challenge of poverty 
eradication a two-pronged strategy has been 
adopted, namely: 
• To bring about macroeconomic stability in 
order to stimulate a rapid growth of incomes 
and employment; and, 
• To build human capital to enable the poor to 
take advantage of new opportunities through 
improving their access to education, health 
and other social services. 
Most of these polices, strategies and programmes 
are in the process of being implemented with the 
assistance of development partners, including 
United Nations system. The areas covered 
include agriculture and natural resource 
development, industrial and infrastructure 
development, the services sector, human 
resource development, advancement of women, 
youth, population, housing, environmental 
protection, private sector development and 
rationalisation and strengthening of private 
sector institutions.
The need for a stable and sound macroeconomic 
environment in promoting poverty eradication 
through the promotion of equitable growth and 
employment creation has been well appreciated 
by the Gambian authorities, and this is evident 
through the economic policies which the 
country has been pursuing, particularly, over the 
past five to six years. 
Between 1985 and 1994, The Gambia embarked 
on a series of structural adjustment programmes 
namely the Economic Recovery Program (ERP) 
and its successor, the Program for Sustained 
Development (PSD). While the ERP sought to 
and addressed the macroeconomic imbalances in 
the 1980s, the PSD was instituted to reinforce 
the gains of the ERP and, in addition, address the 
social dimensions to adjustment neglected under 
the ERP. As a result of the Government’s 
continued focus on improving the welfare of the 
people, this process culminated in the National 
Poverty Alleviation Programme (NPAP) under 
the aegis of Department of State for Finance and 
Economic Affairs. 
The take-over of July 1994, ushered in the 
Armed Forces Provisional Ruling Council

(AFPRC), and brought about a new thinking in 
the Gambia's development priorities. With the 
exception of social sector programmes, several 
donors suspended assistance pending the return 
to democratic constitutional rule. The AFPRC 
designed a development framework known as 
VISION 2020, which it launched in 1997. 
Vision 2020 forms the development policy and 
strategic framework for The Gambia 
3.0 UNDAF GOALS AND 
OBJECTIVES 
The main aim of the UNDAF is to achieve 
greater impact of the UN system cooperation on 
the development and well-being of people 
through improved focus and results orientation, 
identifying where the UN system can make the 
most difference using its unique strengths as a 
development partner. 
The basic goal of the UNDAF is therefore to 
improve the relevance, impact and costeffectiveness of UN assistance at the country 
level. This is done by providing a framework 
with a common perspective, purpose and 
approach to achieve greater impact in response to 
a country’s development priorities as well as the 
agenda emerging from the global conferences 
and UN Conventions, taking into account the 
principles and values of the United Nations. In 
particular, the UNDAF is expected to: 
• overcome fragmentation and overlap 
• allow funds and programmes to function in a 
more unified, co-operative and coherent 
framework, while: 
- maximising effectiveness and impact 
of a modest proportion of the 
resources for development 
- preserving diversity, distinctiveness 
and specialised focus of UN funds 
and programmes. 
The UNDAF provides the strategic framework 
for the preparation, implementation, monitoring 
and evaluation of the individual agency’s 
country programmes. 
In order to realise the goals of the UNDAF for 
The Gambia, namely: to promote human 
development, and the promotion and protection 
of human rights and good governance; a number 
of objectives have by spelt out for each area. 
These areas are summarised in box 1 and box 2, 
below, and will be given further elaboration in United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for The Gambia, 2002 to2006

the individual agency programmes, which will 
be developed following the UNDAF. 
 The promotion of human development 
Promotion and Protection of human rights and good 
governance
4.0 DEVELOPMENT PRIORITIES 
FOR UNDAF 
The CCA and UNDAF processes identified a 
number of key development priorities, and cross 
cutting issues for The Gambia, from the various 
development policies and strategies, as well as 
from commitments emanating from international 
Conferences and Conventions. These were 
verified by the National Workshop on the 
UNDAF, and include the following areas: 
Capacity Building in Economic 
management; 
Governance; 
Poverty Reduction; and 
Environmental Management and Natural 
Resources Development. 
4.1 Capacity Building in Economic 
Management 
Macro-economic stability is seen as the kingpin 
of the Strategy for Poverty Alleviation (SPAII), 
in that it is a necessary condition for sustainable 
growth and for the mobilisation of resources for 
the necessary investment in social infrastructure 
and therefore combating poverty. As such, the 
government places great emphasis on building 
capacities for the analysis, formulation, 
implementation and monitoring and evaluation 
of policies that will promote macroeconomic 
stability. To this end, the country developed a 
12-year economic management programme that 
was presented and endorsed at a Round Table 
conference in 1992. The programme placed 
emphasis on enhancing capacity at the 
Department of State for Finance and Economic 
Affairs (DOSFEA) in the areas of budgeting, 
accounting, financial management, auditing and 
resource mobilisation. In addition, strengthening 
of sectoral budgeting and planning units and 
building local training capacity in the said areas, 
were also key objectives of the programme. 
To underpin sound macro-economic 
management, GOTG formulated its own 
economic long-term strategy, the Vision 2020 in 
1996. To serve as a short-term guideline for the 
implementation of the Vision 2020 objectives, 
the Programme Policy Framework Paper was 
designed and formulated and in 1998 an ESAF 
Programme was negotiated with the IMF 
covering the period 1998 to 2001. 
The ESAF Programme, now known as the 
Poverty Reduction and Growth Facility (PRGF), 
has four broad policy objectives, namely:
To achieve an annual growth rate of 4.5% to 
5% by year 2000. 
To keep inflation at around 3%. 
To reduce the current account deficit to less 
than 10% by the year 2000. 
To keep gross official reserves above five 
months of import cover. 
To maintain a liberal trade policy. 
Macroeconomic management in the Gambia has 
been very commendable over the past five years 
or so. Real GDP has averaged around 5 percent 
between 1996 and 1999. During the same period 
the rate of inflation dropped from 7.0 per cent in 
1995 to 0.9 per cent at the end of 1999, while the 
fiscal deficit ( excluding grants) dropped from 12

The UN system has been supporting the GOTG 
in these efforts, for example, through the UNDP 
supported Economic Management and Capacity 
Building Program (EMCBP 1) and the EMCBP 
II, which is now in its final stages of

During the UNDAF, the UNCT will focus its 
support in the following areas: 
♦ Strengthening policy analysis, formulation , 
monitoring and evaluation, through training 
and technical assistance; 
♦ Improving the consumer price index and rebasing the national accounts; 
♦ Monitoring Government expenditure trends 
through public expenditure reviews (PERs) 
and building capacities for fiscal 
management 
♦ Assist in promoting a conducive

♦ Advocate for and assist in the formulation of 
gender sensitive economic policies.

4.2 Governance 
Good governance constitutes the promotion of 
political participation by all, at all levels, rather 
than merely at multiparty elections, as well as 
adherence to the rule of law, democracy and

4.5.1 Human Rights 
This UNDAF – Gambia has been prepared using 
a rights-based approach for programming of 
development assistance. Human rights relate 
strongly to other major crosscutting issues like 
poverty, gender, population and good 
governance. There are a number of international 
conventions that aim at ensuring the enjoyment 
of the basic universal human rights by all 
segments of the population and in some cases 
specific disadvantaged groups or categories are 
given special attention. All these rights have 
common guiding principles of universality and 
no-discrimination; indivisibility; and 
interdependence. 
The Gambia has a long way to go and has many 
programmes nested in the Vision 2020. 
However, for any of these programmes to be a 
reality, The Gambia Government is very 
cognisant of the importance and need for 
political support and commitment. The 1997 
Constitution provides for the protection of 
fundamental rights and freedom to be enforced 
by the courts. These rights include the protection 
of personal liberty, the protection of personal 
property and protection from discrimination. 
The body of human rights instruments ratified by 
The Gambia forms a legally binding 
development agenda, which the UN system can 
through the UNDAF process use in the 
development of programmes and projects. The 
requirements for the preparation of initial 
reports, periodic reports and monitoring and 
evaluation reports are areas that the Gambia 
Government needs to address to ensure 
compliance. Currently, three reports for CCPR, 
two for CEDAW, ten for CERD, two for CESCR 
and one progress report for CRC are all 
outstanding from the Government. 
The Gambia is a signatory to all major 
international conventions and declarations 
including International Covenant on Economic, 
Social and Cultural Rights (CESCR); 
International Convention on Civil and Political 
Rights (CCPR); International Convention on the 
Elimination of All forms of Racial 
Discrimination (CERD); International 
Convention on the Elimination of All forms of 
Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW); 
Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC); 
ILO Convention on the Elimination of the Worst 
Forms of Child Labour; African Charter on 
Human and People’s Rights, the African Charter 
on the Rights of the Child, the UN Convention 
relating to the status of refugees, and the OAU 
Convention governing the specific aspects of 
refugees. 
The Government of the Gambia has ratified and 
signed these conventions on human and people’s 
rights. However, as at June 2000, there were 
eighteen outstanding conventions whose 
provisions have still not been implemented. The 
UN agencies in The Gambia are supporting the

4.5.2 Gender 
Culturally, men and women have been accorded 
different traditional roles in society. Such roles 
include women working in the household as 
housewives, which act as a deterrent to their 
social and economic advancement. Other 
deterrents are the lack of access to land and 
ownership of productive resources, lack of 
opportunities for paid employment and credit 
facilities, education, skills training and health 
care. 
The UN system has actively supported women in 
an effort to improve gender equity. As part of its 
programmes, UNDP supported capacity building 
at Central Statistics and the Women’s Bureau 
through the Economic Management and 
Capacity Building Project (EMCBP). Support 
was also provided by the UN system for 
Women’s Policy and Council Act elaboration; 
and gender projects targeting women such as 
education, functional literacy, horticulture, 
livestock and income generation and maternal 
and adolescent health have been undertaken. 
Efforts continue to be made to mainstream 
gender issues in the development process in the 
country. In 1980 the National Women’s Bureau 
and Council were established as a national 
advocacy institutions for mainstreaming gender. 
In addition the 1996 Constitution has addressed 
some of the issues of CEDAW in providing 
equal access to education and political rights to 
vote and be voted in parliament. The Gambia has 
also made some progress towards political 
empowerment of women with the appointment 
of a number of female Secretaries of State, 
including the Vice President of the country. 
The Gender-Related Development Indices, i.e. 
the Gender-Related Development Index (GDI), 
and the Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) 
are both low for The Gambia, at 0.384 and 0.242 
(1998), respectively. However, the indices show 
a positive improvement for women and girls in 
the areas of social, economic and political 
development in the country. 
The UN system has developed strategies and 
programmes to address issues emanating from 
gender imbalances and lack of opportunities for 
the girl child. UNICEF in collaboration with 
UNESCO and the World Bank is supporting the 
implementation of the girls education initiative. 
Already, UNICEF and UNFPA have 
successfully concluded a strategy discussion 
with the Government, which has embraced the 
rights-based approach population, to 
development with particular emphasis on 
women, children and the girl child.

 UNICEF’s strategy for HIV/AIDS includes

provide HIV/AIDS prevention, treatment and 
care services at all levels as well as in a number
